  A Long Steep: The History of Tea

  Tea is one of the few beverages that can claim both daily intimacy and civilizational scale. Billions of people drink it for comfort, ritual, medicine, or
  mere habit, yet its story stretches across millennia of agriculture, empire, religion, trade, and taste. To follow tea from a Chinese forest plant to a
  global commodity is to follow the movement of people, ships, and ideas. What follows is a history of that journey—how a leaf became a language spoken in
  cups from Hangzhou to London, Kyoto to Kolkata, Nairobi to Buenos Aires.

  Origins in China

  Most historians place tea’s botanical and cultural origins in southwest China, especially the region encompassing Yunnan and neighboring highland zones
  where Camellia sinensis grows wild. The plant is an evergreen shrub; its leaves, when processed in different ways, yield green, white, oolong, black, and
  dark fermented teas. Long before tea was a packaged product, it was a local resource: chewed, boiled
